title: Dependency and Tool Management
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose of dependency and tool management and explain at least one listed subtopic.
Interpret the example related to dependency and tool management and predict its expected result.
Identify one validation, compatibility, security, or troubleshooting consideration relevant to the example.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will explore dependency and tool management within Professional XML Engineering. You will connect its syllabus topics to an inspectable example, check the expected result, and note tool/version limits.
content.why_it_matters: Dependency and Tool Management matters because XML workflows rely on explicit structure and predictable processing. The lesson helps you reason about parser libraries, avoid a common misunderstanding, and make a result reproducible for another developer.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Professional XML work treats schemas and example documents as versioned contracts. Compatibility decisions should be explicit: identify required/optional fields, unknown-field behavior, migration rules, dependencies, and reproducible verification.

content_blocks.title: Connect the subtopics
content_blocks.text: This lesson explicitly covers: Parser libraries; XSD and XSLT processor dependencies; Version pinning; Reproducible builds; Security updates. Treat these as connected parts of one workflow: define the structure, make the relevant assumptions explicit, and verify a result with a small known input.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: Dependency and Tool Management
content_blocks.expected_output: The sample uses consistent casing and identifiers, separates schema from instance data, and provides a version marker that can be governed through a documented contract process.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Inspect this example as text. Run it only in a processor that supports the shown language/version; the standard CodeLeaf playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only and does not execute XML, XSD, XPath, XSLT, XQuery, Python, or SQL. For a migration, define a mapping from every old field to a new field, keep the original input, validate the generated document against the target schema, compare expected results, and document the compatibility window.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the sample to its exact starting state before each experiment. Change one element, attribute, expression, or constraint at a time, then compare the result with the expected behavior.
content_blocks.limitations: This snippet is an inspectable example, not an XML execution service. Validate it with a standards-compatible XML processor; feature support depends on the processor/version.

content_blocks.title: Version and safety checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Distinguish well-formedness, schema validity, and application-level correctness; they are different checks.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small synthetic example that demonstrates “Parser libraries”. Then add one boundary case involving “XSD and XSLT processor dependencies”. Write down what should happen before testing, and record the exact output or processor message afterward.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a document is correct because it looks readable.
common_mistakes.why: Visual appearance does not prove well-formedness, schema validity, correct namespace handling, or application-level meaning.
common_mistakes.fix: Parse and validate the document with the intended processor, then assert its meaning using a focused test.

common_mistakes.problem: Mixing specification features with processor support.
common_mistakes.why: A standard may define features that a specific runtime does not implement.
common_mistakes.fix: Record the version and feature support; test with the actual target processor.

common_mistakes.why: Missing values, wrong types, namespace differences, or boundary inputs can expose failures.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a valid case, an invalid case, and an edge case to the verification notes.
